implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core supplies the pattern directly: a middleware is a RequestDelegate wrapper registered with app.Use(async (context, next) => { /* pre */ await next(context); /* post */ }), the framework builds the chain in registration order, and app.Run(...) installs the terminal delegate that acts as the target. Registration order is significant - exception handling early, then routing, authentication and authorization - and a middleware that does not call next short-circuits the pipeline.
pitfalls: Calling next after the response has started throws or corrupts the body: check context.Response.HasStarted before any post-processing that writes.
A middleware registered after app.Run(...) is never executed - the terminal delegate ends the pipeline silently.
Middleware are singletons; a scoped service such as a DbContext must be resolved from context.RequestServices per request, not captured in the constructor.

variants.name: ASP.NET Core MVC action filters
variants.idiom_name: IAsyncActionFilter / ActionFilterAttribute in the MVC filter pipeline
variants.implementation_notes: MVC adds a second, attribute-scoped chain inside the middleware pipeline: authorization, resource, action, exception and result filters run around the action, and IAsyncActionFilter's OnActionExecutionAsync receives an ActionExecutionDelegate next whose invocation is the continuation. Global filters surround controller-level filters, which surround method-level filters, so the before/after order follows the scope nesting. Prefer these filters when the concern needs action metadata (ActionDescriptor, model state, attributes); use middleware when the concern is transport-level or must cover non-MVC endpoints such as static files.
pitfalls: Filters run inside the middleware pipeline, so they cannot protect static files or endpoints that never reach MVC.
The five filter kinds have a fixed order and short-circuit differently; assuming a custom attribute runs before authorization is a common misread.
Implement either the synchronous or the asynchronous interface for a stage, not both - the runtime silently ignores the synchronous methods when both exist.
